title: Recursion + Caesar Cipher (OOP)
overview:
**Problem Set 4 — Recursion + a one-time-pad cipher.** Part A is pure recursion over a binary tree (a `Node` class is provided). Parts B and C are object-oriented: a `Message` base class, a `PlaintextMessage` subclass that encrypts with a randomly generated pad, and an `EncryptedMessage` subclass that decrypts. Part C then brute-forces a message against a list of candidate pads and (checkoff-only) decodes a hidden story.

Randomness note: `generate_pad` uses `random.randint`. The test harness seeds `random.seed(0)` before every test, so the pad values are deterministic — every expected value below was computed under seed 0. Source: MIT OCW 6.100L Fall 2022, Problem Set 4 (statements and provided/starter code from OCW; reference solutions and tests written and validated for this study tool).

problems.title: Part A — find_tree_height
problems.statement:
Implement `find_tree_height(tree)` recursively. The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

- A single node (a leaf) has height **0**.
- A tree whose root has children has height `1 + max(height of its subtrees)`.

The provided `Node` class (top of the editor, do not modify) gives you `get_left_child()`, `get_right_child()` — each returns a child `Node` or `None` — and `get_value()`.

The clean base case is the *empty* subtree: define the height of `None` as `-1`, so a single leaf works out to `1 + max(-1, -1) = 0` with no special-casing.

problems.title: Part A — is_heap
problems.statement:
Implement `is_heap(tree, compare_func)` recursively. `compare_func(child_value, parent_value)` returns `True` when the child correctly relates to its parent for the kind of heap being checked:

- **Max heap:** `compare_func = lambda child, parent: child < parent` (every child less than its parent).
- **Min heap:** `compare_func = lambda child, parent: child > parent` (every child greater than its parent).

Return `True` only if **every** parent/child pair in the whole tree satisfies `compare_func`. A single node with no children is trivially a heap.

For each existing child: check `compare_func(child.get_value(), tree.get_value())`, then recurse into that child. The first violation makes the whole tree `False`.

problems.title: Part B — Message.shift_char
problems.statement:
Start the cipher. A `Message` holds text and can shift a single character. Implement the `Message` class so that:

- `Message(text)` stores the text; `get_text()` returns it.
- `shift_char(char, shift)` returns `char` shifted by `shift` positions, **wrapping around within the printable ASCII range 32–126** (95 characters total). Shifting `'~'` (126) forward by 1 wraps to `' '` (32); shifting `' '` back by 1 wraps to `'~'`.

The wrap formula: map the character into `0..94` by subtracting 32, add the shift, take `% 95`, then add 32 back and `chr(...)`. `% 95` handles both positive and negative shifts correctly in Python.

- `shift_char('A', 5)` → `'F'`
- `shift_char(' ', -1)` → `'~'`
- `shift_char('}', 99)` → `'"'`

problems.title: Part B — Message.apply_pad
problems.statement:
Extend `Message` with `apply_pad(pad)`. A **one-time pad** is a list of integers, one per character of the message. Encrypt by shifting the character at index `i` by `pad[i]` (using `shift_char`), and return the resulting ciphertext string. You may assume `len(pad) == len(self.get_text())`.

Build the result by shifting each character in order and joining. Because `apply_pad` reuses `shift_char`, the wrap-around is already handled.

- Applying `[84, 69, 6, ...]` to `'testing message'` produces `'iKyy~(ho1<7A>[3'`.

The `Message` class from the previous problem (with `shift_char`) is provided at the top so you can focus on `apply_pad`.

problems.title: Part B — PlaintextMessage (inheritance + random pad)
problems.statement:
Build `PlaintextMessage`, a subclass of `Message` that encrypts itself on construction.

`PlaintextMessage(input_text, pad=None)`:
- Calls the `Message` constructor (so `get_text()` works via inheritance).
- If `pad is None`, generate one with `generate_pad()`; otherwise store a **copy** of the given pad (so later mutation of the caller's list can't corrupt this object).
- Compute and store the ciphertext = `apply_pad(pad)`.

Methods:
- `generate_pad()` — return a new list with one `random.randint(0, 109)` per character of the text (range `[0, 110)`).
- `get_pad()` — return a **copy** of the pad.
- `get_ciphertext()` — return the stored ciphertext.
- `change_pad(new_pad)` — replace the pad (store a copy) and recompute the ciphertext.

Randomness is deterministic here: the harness runs `random.seed(0)` before each test, so `generate_pad()` on `'he,(llo)'` yields exactly `[108, 49, 97, 53, 5, 33, 65, 62]`.

**Copy discipline matters:** `get_pad()` must not hand out the internal list, and the constructor must not alias the caller's list — otherwise mutating one corrupts the other.

problems.title: Part B — EncryptedMessage.decrypt_message
problems.statement:
Build `EncryptedMessage`, a subclass of `Message` holding ciphertext. Implement `decrypt_message(pad)`: given the pad that was used to encrypt this message, recover the original plaintext and return it as a **`PlaintextMessage`** carrying that pad.

Decryption is just encryption with the **negated** pad: if encrypting shifted each char by `pad[i]`, decrypting shifts by `-pad[i]`. So `apply_pad([-p for p in pad])` on the ciphertext gives the plaintext string; wrap it in `PlaintextMessage(plaintext, pad)` and return that.

- `EncryptedMessage('Monoo#').decrypt_message([5, 10, 2, 3, 0, 2]).get_text()` → `'Hello!'`

The `Message` and `PlaintextMessage` classes are provided at the top; you only write `EncryptedMessage`.

tests.name: decrypt returns a PlaintextMessage carrying the pad

problems.title: Part C — decrypt_message_try_pads
problems.statement:
Brute-force the pad. Given an `EncryptedMessage` and a list of candidate pads, find the pad that decrypts it into the most valid English words.

For each candidate pad: decrypt the ciphertext, split the plaintext on spaces, and count how many tokens are valid words (via the provided `is_word`, which strips punctuation and lowercases). Keep the pad that yields the **most** valid words; on ties, keep the **last** one seen (so iterate in order and use `>=`). Return the winning **`PlaintextMessage`**.

Helpers are provided: `load_words`, `is_word`, and the whole Part B class hierarchy is imported from the provided `ps4b.py` module (so `import ps4b` works and you can use `ps4b.EncryptedMessage`, `ps4b.PlaintextMessage`, etc.). `words.txt` is the dictionary.

- Among six pads for `'Monoo#'`, the pad `[5, 10, 2, 3, 0, 2]` decrypts to `'Hello!'` (1 valid word) and wins.
- If **no** pad produces any valid word, the tie-on-`>=` rule returns the **last** pad's decryption.

problems.solution:
import ps4b

def load_words(file_name):
    with open(file_name, 'r') as inFile:
        wordlist = []
        for line in inFile:
            wordlist.extend([word.lower() for word in line.split(' ')])
        return wordlist

def is_word(word_list, word):
    word = word.strip(" !@#$%^&*()-_+={}[]|\\:;'<>?,./\"").lower()
    return word in word_list

WORDLIST_FILENAME = 'words.txt'
_WORDS = load_words(WORDLIST_FILENAME)

def decrypt_message_try_pads(ciphertext, pads):
    best_msg = None
    best_count = -1
    for pad in pads:
        pm = ciphertext.decrypt_message(pad)
        text = pm.get_text()
        count = sum(1 for token in text.split(' ') if is_word(_WORDS, token))
        if count >= best_count:   # >= keeps the LAST pad on a tie
            best_count = count
            best_msg = pm
    return best_msg

problems.title: Part C — decode_story (study-only)
problems.statement:
The final checkoff task: decode Bob's hidden story. This reads `story.txt` (the ciphertext) and `pads.txt` (a JSON list of candidate pads), builds an `EncryptedMessage`, and runs `decrypt_message_try_pads` against every candidate pad to recover the plaintext.

This is **study-only** here (as it is checkoff-only in OCW): the output is a full paragraph judged by reading it, so there's no crisp unit test. Read the reference solution to see how the earlier pieces compose, then run it in the workspace against the bundled `story.txt`/`pads.txt` to see the decoded story.
